source: Wang, Jain, Zhang, Ray, Kumar, Athiwaratkun (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: At equal budget, chain-of-thought self-consistency (SC) often beats or matches multi-agent debate, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, Least-to-Most and Progressive Hint. With GPT-3.5 on Game of 24, Tree of Thoughts lags SC by a wide margin. With GPT-4, ToT beats everything, even at matched budget, but needs a large budget.
numbers: Five datasets (GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, CSQA, HotpotQA), 100 sampled questions each; Game of 24 uses the same 100 problems as ToT. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023 versions). Budget measured in queries and in tokens.
quote: when scaled to match the compute resources of more sophisticated methods ... this baseline strategy often outperforms them
limits: Old models, 100 questions per set, no 2025-26 reasoning models. The ToT result flips with the model, so the gain is not general. GPT-3.5 needed a modified evaluator prompt.
agent_relevance: Tree search must be compared to SC at equal tokens, and its win depends on the base model. Run that check on our model before relying on S6 ranking.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: ToT component ablation and evaluator cost (Game of 24)
finding: Using a cheap GPT-3.5 evaluator inside a GPT-4-proposer ToT keeps most of the accuracy at about one fifth of the cost. Self-evaluation accuracy depends on the dataset.
numbers: ToT b=5, GPT-4 proposer: GPT-3.5 evaluator 72% for $33.53; GPT-4 evaluator 76% for $159.87 (about 4.8x the cost). GPT-4 evaluator at b=1: 65% for $49.9. Self-evaluation check on 160 balanced answers (80 questions, one right and one wrong each): GPT-3.5 direct 50.6% (chance), with CoT 54.4%; GPT-4 direct 78.75%, with CoT 79.4%. On TheoremQA GPT-4 self-evaluation is close to random. Yes/No format was the best calibrated of Yes/No, 1-10 score, probability.
limits: Game of 24 only for the cost numbers; 100 problems; 2023 API prices; the 160-answer evaluation sample is small.
agent_relevance: A cheap scorer can rank children at S6 with little loss (gap 7 partly closed). Use yes/no scoring rather than 1-10, and do not trust self-scores on hard tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Reflexion with oracle versus self-evaluator, and SC2
finding: An oracle evaluator lifts Reflexion well above SC, but a GPT-4 evaluator leaves it below Reflexion with SC. The authors say reflection is only slightly better than random guessing. Self-confidence-weighted SC (SC2) beats SC on GSM8K and MATH and loses on the other three sets.
numbers: Figure 10 (GPT-4 Reflexion): oracle far above SC; GPT-4 evaluator below SC. SC2 wins on 2 of 5 datasets, loses on 3. Figure values were not extracted as numbers.
limits: Direction only; exact figure values not read.
agent_relevance: The distance between a perfect and a self-made evaluator is the main limit on ranking children at S6.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: With a process reward model (PRM) on MATH, beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets, but the gain shrinks and often reverses as budget grows. Lookahead search usually does worse than the others at the same generation budget. Beam search hurts on easy questions (levels 1-2) and helps on harder ones (levels 3-4); nothing helps on level 5. Choosing the method by predicted difficulty matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* base, MATH test, budgets up to 256 generations. Compute-optimal search roughly equals best-of-N at 64 generations while using 16 (4x saving) at low budget; the saving shrinks with predicted difficulty at high budget.
quote: beam search significantly outperforms best-of-N. However, as the budget is scaled up, these improvements greatly diminish
limits: One base-model family, a PRM trained by the authors, MATH only. Authors blame PRM exploitation: search found repetitive low-information steps and 1-2 step answers.
agent_relevance: More search against an imperfect scorer can lower quality (a Goodhart effect). Cap breadth and depth, use search only on hard items, skip it on easy ones. Direct support for a stopping rule.

source: Wu, Sun, Li, Welleck, Yang (2024/2025) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference (ICLR 2025)
finding: At equal inference FLOPs, a cheap tree search (REBASE: a PRM sets how many children each node gets, no rollouts) beats sampling with weighted majority vote or best-of-n, and beats MCTS. MCTS did poorly because it leaves many unfinished solutions and costs more per solution. A small model with the better search can match a larger model.
numbers: Llemma-7B versus 34B on MATH500 and GSM8K: 7B needs about 2x less FLOPs for matching accuracy; Llemma-7B with REBASE beats Llemma-34B with majority voting at all budgets. MCTS was dropped from the GSM8K plot for a poor accuracy-compute trade-off.
limits: Math only, 2024 models, PRM-based. REBASE reward-model cost is not counted in some token axes.
agent_relevance: Search shape matters: rollout-based MCTS is a poor fit at equal compute; a width-allocating best-first scheme is better. Rank children, expand in proportion, no rollouts.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: A process-supervised reward model (PRM) picks better solutions than an outcome-supervised one (ORM) or majority voting, and the gap grows with N. The ORM can be fooled on easy problems: its accuracy dips as samples increase.
numbers: MATH subset, best-of-1860: PRM 78.2%, ORM 72.4%, majority voting 69.6%. PRM beats both at every N. In the small-scale control, process supervision beats outcome supervision at all data scales.
limits: Human step labels (PRM800K) are costly. PRM training used active learning on harder samples, so training sets are not directly comparable (authors run a control). One generator.
agent_relevance: A step-level scorer ranks branches better than a final-answer scorer. S6 should score steps, not only finished answers.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
finding: A PRM trained on automatic step labels (from rollouts, no human labels) beats self-consistency and an ORM as a reranker on GSM8K and MATH for all generators tested. With a strong reward model, mixing in self-consistency can hurt.
numbers: 256 outputs per question. DeepSeek-67B generator with Math-Shepherd: 93.3% GSM8K, 48.1% MATH. Reward models LLaMA2-70B (GSM8K) and LLemma-34B (MATH). On GSM8K adding SC to the PRM lowered accuracy; on MATH it raised it.
limits: Step labels come from the model's own rollouts, so label noise exists. 2023 models; math only.
agent_relevance: Step scores can be made without humans. Do not stack voting on top of a strong ranker without checking: it can reduce accuracy.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math: Small LLMs Can Master Math Reasoning with Self-Evolved Deep Thinking
finding: A 7B policy plus a 7B process preference model inside MCTS reaches o1-level math. The authors say per-step Q-values are too noisy to score steps directly, so they train the scorer on positive-versus-negative step pairs. Against best-of-N with a 10x larger reward model (Qwen2.5-Math-RM-72B) at the same number of solutions, MCTS with the small scorer wins.
numbers: MATH: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 58.8% to 89.4% with 8 trajectories (90.0% at 64); 1.5B 51.2% to 87.8% (88.4% at 64). AIME 2024: 53.3% (8/15 problems), 8.7 points above o1-preview. Saturates around 64 trajectories on MATH, AIME and Olympiad Bench; College Math keeps rising.
limits: A training result (four self-evolution rounds with code-verified steps), not a scaffold. Comparison fixed to 'same number of solutions', not same tokens. Authors' own numbers.
agent_relevance: A small trained scorer can rank steps well at low cost (gap 7). A scaffold without training cannot copy it, but the lesson holds: rank by relative order, not by absolute score.

source: Liu et al. (2024) rStar: Mutual Reasoning Makes Smaller LLMs Stronger Problem-Solvers (self-reward ablation)
finding: Small models (7B) score their own steps at near-random quality. In RAP (the self-reward tree search), replacing the self-evaluated reward with random values barely changes accuracy. rStar swaps self-reward for mutual consistency between two small models and gets large gains.
numbers: Table 6 (RAP, LLaMA2-7B / Mistral-7B) GSM8K: 24.34 / 56.25 with self-reward, 22.90 / 55.50 with random r1, 22.67 / 49.66 with random r2. MultiArith LLaMA2-7B: 57.22 vs 52.78 (random r1) vs 47.22 (random r2). Only 24% of RAP trajectories from LLaMA2-7B on GSM8K were correct after 32 rounds. rStar GSM8K: LLaMA2-7B 12.51 to 63.91, Mistral 36.46 to 81.88, LLaMA3-8B 47.23 to 85.52. RAP saturates and declines after 4 rollouts on LLaMA3-8B-Instruct.
limits: Models are 7-8B, not frontier. Gains come from 32 rollouts plus a second model as discriminator. Self-reward in strong models (GPT-4) was not tested here.
agent_relevance: Self-scoring a branch is only useful if the model is strong enough to judge. For weak or unsure cases, use agreement across independent samples as the ranker instead of self-rating.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*: LLM Self-Training via Process Reward Guided Tree Search
finding: At the same sampling budget, process-reward-guided MCTS beats Self-Consistency and best-of-N (their Figure 2, MATH and SciBench). As a verifier, its value model slightly beats ORM, Math-Shepherd and SC on MATH500 and GSM8K (Mistral-7B MetaMATH).
numbers: Table 3, 256 outputs. GSM8K: SC 83.9, ORM 86.2, SC+ORM 86.6, Math-Shepherd 87.1, SC+MS 86.3, ReST-MCTS value 87.5 (cell alignment from text extraction). MATH500: SC 35.1, ORM 36.4, SC+ORM 38.0, MS 37.3, SC+MS 38.3, ReST value 39.0. Best PRM over SC: +3.6 GSM8K, +3.9 MATH500.
limits: Same authors built the search and the value model. Gaps among PRMs are small (0.4 to 1.7 points) and no variance is reported. The equal-budget search curve is a figure, not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: Learned step scorers beat plain voting by about 4 points in this setup. The gap among scorers is small, so a cheap one may be enough.

source: Inoue, Misaki, Imajuku, Kuroki, Nakamura, Akiba (2025) Wider or Deeper? Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS), NeurIPS 2025 spotlight
finding: At the same generation budget (27 calls) with external feedback (test scores), plain repeated sampling is a strong baseline. Standard MCTS does not beat it on most settings. Only adaptive branching gets a small edge on coding. On ARC-AGI repeated sampling is best of all.
numbers: Table 1, GPT-4o / DeepSeek-V3. LiveCodeBench: repeated sampling 37.8 / 40.7, standard MCTS 36.7 / 43.2, AB-MCTS-M 38.9 / 43.0, AB-MCTS-A (Gaussian) 39.1 / 42.5. CodeContest: 37.9 / 43.2 vs standard MCTS 37.5 / 43.8 vs AB-MCTS-M 40.6 / 44.6. ARC-AGI: repeated sampling 15.0 / 18.6 (rank 1) vs standard MCTS 9.0 / 14.0 vs AB-MCTS-M 12.3 / 16.0. Average rank: repeated sampling 3.5, standard MCTS 4.2, AB-MCTS-M 2.3, sequential refinement 5.5.
limits: Gains of 1-3 points with SDs from 0.5 to 3.6. Budget is equal in calls, not tokens. GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 are not reasoning models. The scorer is code execution or a grid check, not an LLM.
agent_relevance: At equal calls on coding and puzzle tasks, tree search with a real feedback signal barely beats repeated sampling, and fixed-width MCTS can lose. Use a repeated-sampling arm as the control. Gap 1 stays open for reasoning models.

source: Balachandran et al. (Microsoft Research, 2025) Inference-Time Scaling for Complex Tasks: Where We Stand and What Lies Ahead
finding: On nine models (including o1, o3-mini, GPT-4o) and eight hard tasks, extra tokens do not always buy accuracy. A conventional model with a perfect verifier and many calls can approach the average of a reasoning model on some tasks. Whether parallel or sequential scaling is better depends on the task.
numbers: Best-of-5 gives gains of 10 to 15 points for most models on some tasks. GPT-4o on TSP-easy: 42% to 95% with sequential scaling to 32 calls (best-of-n). On AIME 2025, best-of-n rises linearly in log calls up to 256 parallel calls.
limits: Parallel and sequential scaling, not tree search. Perfect verifiers give upper bounds that a real agent lacks. About 100 instances for some tasks.
agent_relevance: The scorer, not the search shape, sets the ceiling. Supports gap 1 only indirectly: ToT-style search with 2025 reasoning models was not tested.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR 2024; also Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency (arXiv 2305.11860, abstract and intro read)
finding: A simple stopping rule on sampling (stop when a window of answers all agree, or when the vote is lopsided) saves most samples with little accuracy loss.
numbers: ESC cuts average samples by MATH 33.8%, GSM8K 80.1%, StrategyQA 76.8%, CommonsenseQA 78.5%, Coin Flip 84.2%, Last Letters 67.4%, with comparable accuracy. Adaptive-Consistency (17 datasets, 3 LLMs) cuts the budget by up to 7.9x with under 0.1% average accuracy drop.
limits: Both test voting, not tree search. The saving is smallest on the hardest set (MATH, 33.8%). Authors' own numbers; accuracy is called 'comparable', not tested.
agent_relevance: A stopping rule for S6: stop expanding when the top candidates agree. Hard problems get most budget; easy ones stop early (gap 5 partly closed on math and commonsense; not agent tasks).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample right) grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. With automatic verifiers (tests, proof checkers) that turns into accuracy. Without a verifier, majority voting and reward models plateau after about 100 to several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the 43% single-sample state of the art at the time. Reward-model-weighted voting (ArmoRM-Llama3-8B) and plain voting both plateau on 10,000-sample pools of Llama-3-8B and 70B.
limits: Repeated sampling, not tree search. Coding gains need a verifier. Without one, coverage is only an upper bound.
agent_relevance: The ranker is the bottleneck. Where an exact check exists (code, tests), prefer it to any LLM score. Where none exists, expect ranking gains to flatten.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as a self-verifier is unreliable. High false negative rates make the loop worse than one try on graph coloring and Mystery Blocksworld. The false positive rate (accepting a wrong answer, an overestimate proxy) is lower: 0.5% to 18.55%.
numbers: Table 2 (accuracy / false positive rate / false negative rate): Game of 24 87.0% (3567/4100), 10.4%, 20.7%; Graph Coloring 72.4% (362/500), 6.5%, 95.8% (113/118); Blocksworld 71.8% (359/500), 18.55%, 15.48%; Mystery Blocksworld 79.6% (398/500), 0.5%, 97.09% (100/103). In Game of 24 it called 79.1% of correct equations correct yet evaluated 81.6% of them to 24.
limits: GPT-4 only (2023). Binary accept/reject, not ranking of states. 100 instances per domain for the loop runs. The Table 1 cells were not used because the layout text was ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Under-acceptance is the dominant error: the model throws away right answers. A prune step that relies on self-critique will cut real solutions (as in the ToT crossword note). Use a sound check where one exists.

source: Hart, Nilsson, Raphael (1968) A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths, IEEE Trans. SSC 4(2), 100-107
finding: Read from page images (scanned PDF, no OCR text), pages 104-106. Admissible means h never exceeds the true remaining cost. The consistency assumption (their eq. 5, a triangle inequality h(m)<=k(m,n)+h(n)) gives: a closed node's g is already optimal, so A* never reopens nodes (Lemma 2), and f is nondecreasing over closed nodes (Lemma 3). Theorem 2: any admissible algorithm no more informed than A* expands every node A* expands (no-ties case). Theorem 3 extends it to ties: some tie-breaking of A* expands only nodes the other algorithm also expands. Corollary 2 bounds extra work from ties by the number of critical ties.
numbers: Theorems 2 and 3 and their corollaries all assume the consistency assumption and delta graphs (arc costs bounded below by a positive number). Fig. 2 example: inconsistent estimates h(s)=8 and h(n2)=1 make A* expand the wrong node.
quote: A* is an optimal algorithm. Compared with other no more informed admissible algorithms, it expands the fewest possible nodes
limits: The optimality theorems are stated under consistency, not admissibility alone. The paper says nothing about noisy scores. Dechter and Pearl (1985) generalise to inconsistent h; not opened. Pearl 1984 book not opened.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'theorems rest on Wikipedia' point for the main result. The guarantee needs a lower-bounding score. An LLM rating has no such property, so S6 should be called a ranking aid, not an optimal search.

source: Wilt and Ruml (2012) When does Weighted A* Fail? SoCS-12
finding: Raising the weight in Weighted A* (and going greedy) does not always speed up search. In some domains greedy search expands more nodes than A*. The paper tests several explanations (heuristic percent error, local-minimum size, h-versus-h* correlation) and rejects them. Greedy search is fast only if h correlates strongly with the true distance-to-go d(n), or h is extremely accurate.
numbers: Greedy works: Towers of Hanoi, grid, pancake, dynamic robot, unit-cost 11-tile, TopSpin(3); h-d Spearman 0.94, 0.97, 0.96, 0.997, 0.71, 0.52. Greedy fails: TopSpin(4), inverse-cost tiles, City Navigation 3x3 and 4x4; h-d Spearman 0.39, 0.34, -0.03, 0.16. Percent error does not separate the two groups (Hanoi 29.47% works but inverse-cost tiles 29.49% fails; unit tiles 33.4% works; City Nav 4x4 37.4% and 3x3 44.5% fail). h-versus-h* Spearman does not either (TopSpin(3) 0.52 works; City Nav 0.61 and 0.75 fail). In TopSpin(4) and City Navigation 3x3 greedy expands more nodes than A*. City Nav 5x5 has weak h-d correlation (Pearson 0.09) yet greedy is fine because h tracks h* at 0.95.
quote: greedy search is fast if and only if there is a strong correlation between h(n) and d(n)
limits: Counts nodes expanded, not wall-clock or solution cost. Small benchmark domains. Table columns were realigned by hand (10 domains, values read in order). Correlation explains after the fact; it is not a test to run before search. Paper found on the author's page.
agent_relevance: Ranking children by a score fails when the score orders nodes by the wrong thing. Rank agreement with distance-to-goal, not the size of the score error, predicts whether greedy ranking works. Measure the Spearman between our child scores and true steps-to-solve on a dev set before trusting greedy ranking at S6.

source: Helmert and Roger (2008) How Good is Almost Perfect? AAAI-08
finding: Even a heuristic that is almost perfect (absolute error bounded by a small constant c) forces A* to expand exponentially many states on common planning domains. In GRIPPER and MICONIC there is no big difference between A* with error 1 and breadth-first search. BLOCKSWORLD gets the same result through a family of independent subproblems. Pohl's linear-time result for constant error rests on assumptions (constant branching factor, one optimal path) that planning tasks break.
numbers: Theorem 1: GRIPPER with error 1, about half of all reachable states must be considered. Experiments: GRIPPER and both MICONIC variants grow exponentially even for c=1; BLOCKSWORLD and LOGISTICS show a similar but less clear trend (most visible at c=5).
quote: A* must necessarily explore an exponential number of search nodes even under the optimistic assumption of almost perfect heuristic estimators
limits: Worst-case theorems on a few planning domains; optimal search only, not satisficing or greedy. Not about noisy LLM scores directly.
agent_relevance: Better scores alone do not fix search on tasks with many symmetric, interleavable parts. Gains must come from elsewhere (pruning symmetries, decomposing). Do not expect better child scoring to rescue combinatorial tasks.

source: Li et al. (2024) Q*: Improving Multi-step Reasoning for LLMs with Deliberative Planning, Tables 2-4 re-read from PDF page images
finding: The Q* numbers are real table cells. Q* with a trained Q-value model (QVM) beats best-of-N with the same model, by a small margin on the stronger bases.
numbers: GSM8K (Llama-2-7b + MetaMath): base 65.2; PPO(PRM) 67.2; PPO(QVM) 67.6; best-of-N(PRM) 72.1; best-of-N(QVM) 74.5; Q*(QVM) 78.8; Q*(PRM+QVM) 80.8. ChatGPT-turbo 77.7, GPT-4 5-shot 92.0. MATH: Llama-2-7b Synthetic Data 41.9, PPO 42.5, best-of-N 46.8, Q* 49.1; DeepSeek-Math-7b 50.8, best-of-N 54.3, Q* 55.4 (Gemini Ultra 53.2). MBPP (CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat): 74.6 base, best-of-N 75.0, Q* 77.0 (GPT-4 self-debug 80.2).
limits: Settles correction 2: 74.5% is the best-of-N(QVM) cell and 65.2% is the base, so the paper does not disagree with itself. Q* over best-of-N: +4.3 (GSM8K, QVM only), +2.3 (MATH, Llama), +1.1 (MATH, DeepSeek), +2.0 (MBPP). The 80.8 row (PRM+QVM) has no matching best-of-N with both scorers. Single run, no variance, no matched-token comparison.
agent_relevance: On strong math and code bases the edge of search over best-of-N is only 1 to 2 points. A trained scorer is the main ingredient.

source: van Opheusden et al. (2023) Expertise increases planning depth in human gameplay, Nature (abstract only)
finding: Human moves in four-in-a-row are captured by a heuristic-search model. Planning depth rises with expertise, in lab and in large-scale mobile data. Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC); methods and numbers were not.
numbers: No numbers extracted this session.
limits: Abstract only, so opened is false. Nothing on human heuristic error rates or admissibility. Newell and Simon (1972) was not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Humans use heuristic best-first search and plan deeper with skill; that weakly supports scaling depth, not admissible-like scoring.
